title: Time, days and market days
goal: Tell the time, name the days and the parts of the day — then meet something no Western calendar has: five market days that rotate alongside the ordinary seven.
bekal: tell the time, including the *setengah* (half) pattern that counts forward, not back
name the seven weekdays and the five market days
use *saiki*, *mau*, *mengko*, *wingi*, *sésuk* to place events in time

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Janjian karo Rini
dialogs.intro: Dian and Rini are planning a trip to Malioboro, Yogyakarta's famous shopping street. The talk is ngoko, fast and full of time words — exactly like making real plans.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Ésuk kuliah, awan kosong. Ana apa?
lines.id: Classes in the morning, free in the afternoon. What's up?
lines.literal: morning lecture, midday empty. there-is what?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Aku péngin nyang Malioboro. Melu, ora?
lines.id: I want to go to Malioboro. Coming or not?
lines.literal: I want to Malioboro. join, not?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Rada awan. Setengah papat waé, luwih adhem.
lines.id: A bit too hot then. Let's say half past three, it's cooler.
lines.literal: rather midday. half four just, more cool.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Setengah papat kuwi jam telu luwih telung puluh, ta?
lines.literal: half four that hour three more three ten, right?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Bener. Setengah nuju ing jam papat, dudu setengahé jam papat.
lines.id: Right. It's halfway to four, not half of four.
lines.literal: right. half heading to hour four, not half-of hour four.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Oh, ngono. Sésuk dina apa, ya?
lines.id: Oh, I see. What day is it tomorrow?
lines.literal: oh, like-that. tomorrow day what, yeah?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Setu Kliwon. Pasar Beringharjo rame banget nèk Kliwon.
lines.id: Saturday Kliwon. Beringharjo Market is really busy on Kliwon.
lines.literal: Saturday Kliwon. market Beringharjo busy very if Kliwon.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Dina pasaran. Mengko tak critani ing dalan.
lines.id: A market day. I'll tell you about it on the way.
lines.literal: day market. later I tell-to-you on road.

notes: **Ta** at the end of a sentence asks for confirmation, like English "…, right?" or "isn't it?". *Ya?* does the same job; in East Java *ta?* is said more emphatically.

**Gelem** means "willing, happy to"; krama *purun*. Keep it apart from *arep* (going to, will) and *péngin* (want). *Aku gelem* accepts an invitation; *aku arep* states a plan; *aku péngin* states a wish.
**Melu** means "to come along, join"; krama *ndhèrèk*. *Ndhèrèk* is also a polite phrase when passing through someone's home: *ndhèrèk langkung* (excuse me, may I pass).

**Nèk** is the short form of *menawa* (if, when), and the one you'll hear most. Krama *menawi*. You'll use it in almost every conversation: *nèk ana wektu* (if there's time), *nèk kesel* (if you're tired).
**Tak critani** — the *tak* + verb form from Unit 5, here with the ending *-i*, meaning "to someone". *Tak critani* = "I'll tell you about it". The endings *-i* and *-aké* are covered in Unit 18.
**Rame** means "lively, crowded", and in Java it is almost always positive — busy means alive, fun, full of people. Krama is also *ramé*.

grammars.title: Telling the time: the half that counts forward
body: Telling the time in Javanese is simple — except for one thing you must get right now, because a mix-up here can make you an hour late.
after: **Setengah papat means 3:30, not 4:30.** Javanese counts *halfway towards* four, not "half past" four. Dutch and German work the same way, and the pattern came into Javanese in colonial times.

If you're unsure, avoid it altogether and just say the numbers: *jam telu telung puluh* (three thirty). That's correct, understood and risk-free. But you still need to **understand** *setengah* when others use it — and they will.
**Luwih** (past, literally "more") and **kurang** (to, literally "less") frame the minutes. Krama *langkung* and *kirang*.

sections.title: Weekdays, and the market days turning behind them

blocks.text: The seven ordinary weekdays come from Arabic and Portuguese, like their Indonesian counterparts:

What no Western calendar has is the **pasaran** — a **five-day** cycle running alongside the seven-day week. Its days are **Legi, Pahing, Pon, Wagé, Kliwon**. Because five and seven turn together, any given combination — say *Setu Kliwon* — comes back once every thirty-five days. That thirty-five-day span is called a **selapan**.

Say it
Good to know
rows: often used in the names of markets and village market days
many small towns have a Pon market
considered the most special; *Jemuwah Kliwon* and *Setu Kliwon* carry particular meaning in tradition

blocks.title: Weton: why people ask what day you were born
items: The weekday plus market day of someone's birth is their **weton** — for example *Rebo Pon*. It's used to choose wedding dates, good days to move house, and days for a *selamatan* (ritual communal meal).

If an older person asks *wetonmu apa?*, they want that combination, not the date. The honest answer "kula boten mangertos" (I don't know) is perfectly acceptable — plenty of young Javanese don't know either.
At A1 you don't need to calculate a weton. Just **recognize the five market-day names** when you hear them, so you know *Setu Kliwon* is a day, not a place.

blocks.text: The parts of the day combine with the words above, just as in English ("this morning", "tomorrow night"):
**Sasi** means "month" **and** "moon" — like the two English words, which share a root. When you need the heavenly body specifically, say *rembulan*.
